sense: say that something is not true

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; with an accusative, or an accusative and infinitive
evidence: Ter. Ad. 799: Factum est; nōn negō.
Cic. Fin. 2.68 (Lewis & Short): Stōicī negant quidquam esse bonum, nisi quod honestum sit
terms.comment: The opposite of ajō, to say yes (see say). “He denies he did it” is negat sē fēcisse: Latin puts the negative in the verb and leaves the infinitive positive. The same verb refuses (see deny, refuse).

terms.gloss: deny, disown; refuse to own a debt
evidence: Cic. Cat. 3.11 (Lewis & Short): cum id posset īnfitiārī, repentē cōnfessus est
terms.comment: To deny what one is charged with, the opposite of fatērī; in law, to deny a debt or a deposit (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: phrase: the accusative īnfitiās with forms of īre
terms.register: vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.; in prose Nep., Liv., not Cic.
evidence: Ter. Ad. 339: ille īnfitiās ībit, sat sciō
terms.comment: Mostly with a negative: nēmō it īnfitiās, no one denies it; neque negō neque īnfitiās eō (Liv. 6.40.4). Lewis & Short: not in Cicero or Caesar.
The verb is classical (Cicero, Livy); with a negative it admits a point.

phrases.english: Someone says no? I say no. He says yes? I say yes.
It’s done; I don’t deny it.

sources: Lewis & Short: nego · Lewis & Short: infitior · Lewis & Short: infitiae
Ter. Eun. 252, Ad. 339, 799 and Plaut. Curc. 489 checked against the Perseus Latin texts (11 November 2026).
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 302.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
